ICL—the component responsible for much of the practical success—is deliberately biased: transitions generated at U are used as targets at an interpolated parameter U-hat that itself depends on the sampled action, without a valid correction. There is no characterization of this bias or convergence result for ICL/DA-AC. In the bandit visualization, the learned ICL critic even predicts values far outside the feasible reward range, so useful optimization curvature is being substituted for accurate value estimation.

The theory does not cleanly cover the implementation. The categorical parameter space is a constrained simplex rather than the ordinary full-dimensional action domain assumed by DPG; the Dirac construction used to recover DPG violates the stated continuity assumption; and clipped Gaussian policies contain boundary atoms inconsistent with the density assumptions. Proposition 4.5 also incorrectly writes conditioning on epsilon while purportedly integrating over epsilon.

The experiments do not convincingly attribute benchmark gains to the advertised lower-variance estimator. With exact critics, its advantage is only marginal in two toy bandits; in realistic experiments, DA-PG is inseparable from biased ICL. Sensitivity studies for interpolation, the deterministic endpoint, minimum variance, and importance-corrected alternatives are missing.

The statistical treatment is weaker than the experimental scale suggests. Seed-environment runs are pooled as independent observations, paired t-tests ignore the hierarchical task structure and multiple comparisons, and headline averages use manually normalized final training returns rather than consistently reported evaluation-policy returns.

Reproducibility has avoidable inconsistencies: the main text and tables specify MuJoCo v3 while plots and normalization details specify v4; an actor-target ablation mentions 10 DMC tasks although the study uses 15; and the reproducibility statement promises a code release but provides no URL in the supplied manuscript. The paper includes useful diagnostics and ablations, including bandit visualizations, DA-AC without ICL, comparisons with estimator-matched actor-critic variants, and an actor-target-network study. Hyperparameters and resource requirements are extensively documented.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is overstated. Treating randomized controls as deterministic actions over probability measures is closely related to classical relaxed/measure-valued control, while the exact DA gradient is essentially an expected or marginalized policy gradient. The paper does not adequately position itself against the former literature, and the claim of the first unbiased reparameterization-style estimator for discrete actions is not convincingly established. With a learned DA critic, the practical estimator is not unbiased.

ICL, a central algorithmic ingredient, deliberately trains at a distribution parameter different from the data-generating one without importance correction and is therefore generally biased. The toy plots visibly produce substantially distorted values. There is no analysis of this bias and no comparison against the obvious unbiased endpoint update at U_A, importance weighting, alternative interpolation distributions, or different interpolation schedules.

The theory does not validate the practical algorithm. The variance results require exact critics, whereas DA-AC uses an approximate critic trained with biased ICL. The convergence result is essentially a substitution into an existing on-policy linear-critic result with oracle occupancy sampling and excludes ICL, replay, nonlinear critics, and the off-policy implementation.

There are formal technical problems in the appendix. In Proposition 4.5, the stated conditioning Y=E[X|S_t,epsilon] makes the subsequent total-variance argument incorrect; the intended conditioning is only on S_t. Dirac policies used to claim strict generalization and clipped Gaussians used experimentally also do not cleanly satisfy the stated smooth-density assumptions.

The evaluation omits important comparisons. Hybrid experiments use benchmarks and implementations from the HyAR work but do not compare against HyAR itself. Continuous experiments omit stronger modern methods such as CrossQ despite citing them, and the high-dimensional discretized experiments omit methods specifically designed for discretized continuous control. Hyperparameter-selection protocols are also not reported.

The statistical analysis is not reliable enough for the claims. It pools task-seed observations as independent samples, inflating sample sizes from the number of tasks to as many as 150 observations, rather than using task-level or hierarchical inference. The across-setting test additionally combines dependent settings that reuse the same tasks. Normalization is specified for continuous benchmarks but not clearly defined for Gym, MinAtar, or PAMDP aggregates.

Reproducibility has consequential inconsistencies: the promised code-release location is blank; the text and tables refer to MuJoCo v3 while plots refer to v4; the pseudocode applies a minus sign to the stated return gradient; and most settings use noisy training returns rather than separate evaluation returns.

The claimed universality hides substantial structural assumptions. A categorical distribution over a general combinatorial action space can require exponentially many parameters; the high-dimensional experiments avoid this by imposing independent per-dimension distributions, thereby restricting the policy class. Action-specific parameterizations and sampling functions are still manually required.

The empirical study is unusually broad: continuous, low- and high-dimensional discrete, and hybrid control are evaluated across many tasks, generally with 10 seeds, confidence intervals, individual learning curves, and targeted bandit experiments.

weaknesses: The headline variance result assumes exact action-value functions. ICL—the component responsible for much of the empirical success—is deliberately biased: a transition generated under U is relabeled to a sample-dependent interpolated parameter without correction. ICL is less general than the overarching framework suggests. It requires an observable sampled action and a parameter U_A representing a deterministic distribution; for Gaussian policies, the latter is only approximated using the minimum allowed variance. The paper formally relates the transformed MDP to the original MDP and connects DA-PG to DPG and conditional expectations of likelihood-ratio and reparameterization gradients. Under exact critics, the conditional-variance reduction is meaningful.

The evaluation is unusually broad: 20 continuous-control tasks, nine standard discrete tasks, 20 discretized-control tasks, and seven hybrid-control tasks, generally with 10 seeds. Direct LR, RP, straight-through, expected-gradient, value-based, and hybrid-action comparisons are included.

DA-AC is consistently competitive and appears particularly effective on higher-dimensional DMC, discretized-control, and hybrid benchmarks. The ICL ablation and bandit visualizations provide some useful mechanistic evidence.
The manuscript is clearly organized and supplies extensive hyperparameters, pseudocode, individual learning curves, and resource information.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is limited. DA-PG is essentially DPG applied to a reformulated MDP and, with an exact critic, recovers an expected policy gradient. Closely related concurrent D-MDP work is acknowledged. Claims such as the “first unbiased RP-style estimator” for discrete actions and “strict generalization” therefore need substantially more careful positioning.

The main theory does not validate the practical algorithm. The variance results assume exact critics, while ICL deliberately applies transitions at counterfactual distribution parameters without importance correction and is acknowledged to be biased. The convergence result covers on-policy linear TD without ICL, replay, twin critics, or nonlinear approximation—not the evaluated DA-AC method.

Evidence for ICL remains incomplete. There is no characterization of its bias or ablation of interpolation distributions, endpoint relabeling, importance correction, number of relabeled samples, or action observability. With an oracle critic, DA-PG's advantage in the bandits is only marginal.

Baseline coverage is not fully competitive. Continuous-control comparisons rely mainly on TD3/SAC/PPO, relevant scalable discretization methods are omitted, and HyAR is conspicuously absent from the PAMDP evaluation despite supplying the benchmark protocol. The tuning budget is unclear, and PDQN is evaluated with altered hyperparameters.

The aggregate evaluation has methodological problems: normalization is documented only for MuJoCo/DMC and uses hand-selected maxima; most results use exploratory training returns rather than a common evaluation protocol; task-seed observations are pooled as independent samples in t-tests and bootstraps, ignoring task clustering; and per-task numerical tables are absent.

Reproducibility contains concrete inconsistencies: MuJoCo v3 and v4 are used interchangeably, Figure 11 reports 10 DMC tasks whereas the benchmark has 15, and the supplied PDF has no visible code-release URL. The pseudocode appears to descend rather than ascend the stated Q objective, and Proposition 4.5 conditions on epsilon incorrectly in its written variance decomposition.

Overall, the idea and empirical breadth are promising, but the novelty, theory-to-algorithm gap, missing strong comparisons, and evaluation inconsistencies place the work marginally below the top-tier acceptance threshold.
